title: The bond continues
hook: many keep a bond with the dead, and grief researchers now see it as healthy

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was in waves: grief swinging toward the loss and back to life, not climbing stages. Your line was deep calleth unto deep.

A phone, a name in the contacts, and a message sent anyway: got the job. wish you could see. Nobody will answer. She knows that. She sends it anyway, puts the phone down, and feels a little less alone with the news. Somewhere else a man sets out his father's chair at the holiday table. A woman tells a gravestone about the new baby. For a long time, some schools of psychology would have called all of this a problem, a sign of grief not finished. What changed, and what were some traditions doing all along?
screen: `A TEXT TO A NUMBER THAT WON'T ANSWER.` → `A CHAIR AT THE TABLE.` → `A PROBLEM, OR A BOND?`

segments.voice: First, the older view. Healthy grief meant letting go: slowly loosening your ties to the person who died, so your heart was free to attach elsewhere. Some trace the idea to Freud's essay Mourning and Melancholia. Keeping up a relationship with the dead could look like refusing to accept the death. Second, the turn. The researchers Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman gathered studies of grieving people in a book called Continuing Bonds. People kept a relationship with their dead: talking to them, asking what they would think, carrying their values, feeling them near at a wedding. And this was often part of healthy grieving, not a failure of it. Researchers since have added a fair caution: some bonds comfort and some trouble, depending on the person and the loss. Third, traditions had words for this already. In Jewish custom, after naming someone who has died, people add a short phrase: may their memory be a blessing. In some Japanese Buddhist homes, a household altar called a butsudan holds photos and memorial tablets, and families greet the dead there, offer rice or tea, and tell them the news. Fourth, what continues is not the same as what was. The bond changes shape: from a voice on the phone to a voice in memory, from advice given to advice imagined, from a hand held to a value carried. The relationship moves. It doesn't have to end. The bond continues.
screen: `LET GO, SAID AN OLDER VIEW` · `CONTINUING BONDS` · `MAY THEIR MEMORY BE A BLESSING` · `THE BOND CHANGES SHAPE` · then, large: `THE BOND CONTINUES.`

segments.voice: Choose someone who has died, a person or even an animal, or if no one comes, an ancestor you never met, and let them come to mind as they were on an ordinary day. Silently tell them one thing, a piece of news, a thank-you, a question, then simply sit, the way you would after saying something to a friend across the table, no answer needed. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words.
Butsudan, the household altar in some Japanese Buddhist homes where family members greet their dead and tell them the news. Today's word.
Your line: a voice in memory. Staying in touch can take a new shape. Eight hundred days now.

howItsDone: People keep bonds with the dead in many ways: Jewish families add "may their memory be a blessing" after a name, some Japanese Buddhist households greet the dead at a home altar, and others visit graves, keep a photo, or talk to the person on a walk.

chat.says: Is it unhealthy that I still talk to my grandpa, even though he died?
options: Not necessarily. Researchers found keeping a bond is often part of healthy grief.
Yes. Healthy grief means letting go fully, so your heart is free again.
It's fine for a few weeks, but it should stop once the funeral is over.
